topic: cutting peat on a hill bank: footing the turfs, the bottom spit, building a rickle and stacking at home

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: deszczomierz z odczytem przy glowie banku

base: I took over a peat bank on the hill this spring and cut my first turfs in May.
The turf shed behind the house still holds a few dozen turfs from my uncle's time.
A rain gauge stands at the head of the bank and I read it every week.
I cut about two thousand turfs and laid them flat on the heather to dry.
They are still soft in August, so am I drying them wrongly or simply cutting too late?
Laid flat is the whole trouble, since a turf on its side dries on one face only.
Foot them instead: set three or four on end, leaning together, a week after cutting.
The wind then reaches every face and the water leaves from the whole surface at once.
A footed turf dries in a month where a flat one is still soft at Michaelmas.
I footed the next cutting a week after lifting them and the difference was very plain.
The rain gauge shows barely an inch through June, which must have helped a good deal.
Some turfs at the foot of the bank are still heavy and darker than the rest.
Is that a wetter part of the bank, or did I cut those ones too deep?
Too deep, most likely, because the bottom spit lies below the water and never dries the same.
Black peat from that depth burns longer but wants an extra month standing in the wind.
Keep the bottom spit separate from the top and foot it in rather smaller groups.
Mixing the two in one stack means the good turfs take damp back from the poor ones.
I kept the bottom spit apart and footed it in threes on the driest part of the bank.
By the end of July the top spit rang hollow when I knocked two turfs together.
The turf shed is only half full and I have four cartloads still out on the hill.
The weather has turned and I am anxious about leaving them up there much longer.
Should I bring them home wet, or build a rickle on the bank and wait?
Build the rickle on the bank, since turfs brought home damp will heat and go to dust.
A rickle is loosely built and a stack tightly built, and that difference decides the winter.
Set the turfs on edge in a round heap with the ends outward and a hollow middle.
Rain runs off the outer turfs and the wind still works through the whole heap.
Leave it three weeks and then cart home whatever rings hollow to the knuckle.
The rickle stood three weeks and nearly all of it rang hollow when I came back.
I carted the turfs home and now have the shed full and a good deal left over.
The extra will have to sit outside against the gable through the whole winter.
How should an outdoor stack be built so that the rain does not spoil the lot?
Build it long and narrow rather than square, with the ends of the turfs facing outward.
Slope the sides slightly inward as you rise, so each course sheds water clear of the one below.
Cap it with the poorest turfs laid flat and overlapping, which you can afford to lose.
Never cover a peat stack with sheeting, because what cannot breathe will rot from within.
I built the stack long and narrow and capped it with the worst of the bottom spit.
It has come through the winter and only the cap turfs were spoiled at all.
Next May I want to cut a fresh face rather than work the old one any further.
Where along the bank should a new face be opened, and how wide should it run?
Open the new face at the end of the old one, so the drainage you have made still serves.
Flay the heather off a strip about a yard wide and throw it into the cut ground behind.
A yard is as much as one person can keep dry and lift in a single season.
Work always with the bank on your left and the cut ground filling in behind you.
